source.title: LLM Persona Unlearning
source.authors: Ke-Mou Li; Zhuan Shi; Qi-Zhou Wang; Feng-Peng Li; Negar Rostamzadeh; Golnoosh Farnadi; Jian-Tao Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The paper is read in full and cites refusal-direction work, but its experiments concern persona behavior, not refusal or a refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The study estimates target–counterpart persona directions and edits model weights, but it does not measure refusal, harmful-versus-harmless instruction contrasts, or the refusal direction. These are related persona-direction results, not tests of the listed refusal-claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds same-question target-minus-counterpart persona directions and trains weight edits to suppress personas (sycophantic, hallucinating, impolite, apathetic, evil). It never measures refusal or uses a harmful-minus-harmless direction. Arditi et al. is cited only in related work on steering. The results concern a related but different construct, persona expression, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that PACE consistently suppresses target personas across models, with high response quality and largely preserved counterpart behavior. They report moderate general-utility costs and residual accessibility under stronger elicitation, notably iterative attacks on Sycophantic and Hallucinating.
record.recipe_differences: PACE computes a difference between same-question target- and counterpart-persona response states, selects a layer, then trains a weight edit on target prompt states with projection erasure and counterpart anchoring. It is not harmful-minus-harmless refusal-direction ablation or addition. The paper reports persona unlearning, not abliteration.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports variation by model, persona, selected layer, erasure margin and anchor weight, as well as elicitation setting. For example, PACE's TF falls under iterative attacks for Sycophantic and Hallucinating; translated Impolite prompts retain TF 100.0 in all five tested languages. These sensitivities concern persona unlearning, not refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: A mean-difference direction from same-question target vs. counterpart persona responses was found. Steering against it (coefficient −2) lowers persona expression at selected layers, e.g. Llama Sycophantic 100→56.83, but only 1.5 points for Gemma Hallucinating. A weight edit suppressing this projection achieves high target forgetting at a moderate utility cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive persona directions, analogous to the refusal direction, can be causally relevant and used for weight-level persona suppression. Their causal strength varies by layer, model and persona.

record.problems: The study does not test the refusal claim. Its persona evaluations use a frozen LLM judge; the paper notes that independent judges and human assessment would strengthen evaluation. Reported operating points use one training seed.

untested.parts: No refusal direction, harmful/harmless contrast, ablation or addition affecting refusal, or capability cost of refusal removal.
No abliteration or weight edit removing refusal.
Jailbreak tests concern re-eliciting personas after unlearning, not suppression of a refusal direction.
No multi-direction or cone account of refusal.
Harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are not measured separately.
Cross-lingual tests cover persona unlearning, not transfer of a refusal direction.
Reasoning-before-answering is not studied with respect to refusal.

record.verdict_notes: Some edited outputs (e.g. Llama PACE on Sycophantic and Impolite) become refusal-like ('I can't advise you…'). This is incidental and not measured as refusal, so it does not bear on any version. The direction-steering probe is a persona analogue of V1 but targets persona, not refusal.

versions.untested_parts: No refusal behavior, harmful-minus-harmless direction, refusal ablation, refusal induction, or general-capability cost of removing a refusal direction is tested.
The paper trains weight edits for persona unlearning; it does not test abliteration or weight edits removing refusal.
No attack is tested for suppressing a refusal direction, and no training against refusal-direction ablation is studied.
No affine, cone, or multi-direction account of refusal is tested.
No harmfulness judgment or refusal decision is measured as separate quantities.
Cross-language evaluation concerns persona unlearning, not transfer of a refusal direction; base-to-instruct or refusal-direction transfer is not tested.
The study does not vary refusal training or test whether it determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
Reasoning models and refusal after reasoning are not evaluated.

rows.subject: 12 full-parameter model–persona settings (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: PACE trains model weights using a target–counterpart persona direction, projection erasure, and counterpart anchoring.
rows.baseline: Other compared methods; exact aggregate baseline value not stated.
rows.value: PACE achieves the highest TF in all 12 settings.
rows.note: This is an explicitly reported aggregate result about persona expression, not refusal. The study does not give one aggregate numerical TF value here.
rows.check: The row compares the study's own method (PACE) against other unlearning baselines on persona forgetting. That is a method-performance comparison, not a measure of refusal or of a refusal direction, so it bears on no version. Its state can't be read against any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
